nameStory: Putnam's Jumping Spider honors Frederick Ward Putnam, a 19th-century American naturalist who helped establish the Peabody Museum at Harvard University. Putnam was passionate about cataloging America's natural heritage, making this spider's name a tribute to early scientific exploration. Like many species named for pioneering naturalists, this spider carries forward the legacy of those who first documented our regional biodiversity.
description: Putnam's Jumping Spider is a compact, stocky member of the jumping spider family with the characteristic forward-facing large eyes that give these spiders their alert, almost mammal-like appearance. Like other jumping spiders, it's an active hunter that stalks prey rather than building webs, moving in quick, deliberate jumps. These spiders are relatively small, typically measuring less than half an inch in body length. They're known for their excellent vision and curious behavior, often turning to watch observers with their prominent front eyes.

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large forward-facing eyes arranged in a distinctive pattern, with the two center eyes noticeably larger and giving an almost cartoon-like appearance. The eyes have a glossy, black appearance that seems to track movement.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and robust build with a relatively flat, rectangular carapace (front body section) that feels firm to the touch if handled gently. The abdomen is typically oval and somewhat flattened.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in characteristic quick jumps rather than continuous crawling, often pausing to turn and look directly at observers. Will raise front legs and wave them when threatened or displaying.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length typically ranges from 8-12mm, roughly the size of a small fingernail. Legs are proportionally shorter and sturdier than those of web-building spiders.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Coloration and patterns can be variable, but typically shows darker markings on a lighter background. The carapace often has a subtle metallic sheen when viewed in good light.

habitat: Putnam's Jumping Spider can be found in a variety of habitats throughout New England, from woodland edges to gardens and fields. They prefer areas with some vegetation structure like low shrubs, fence posts, or rock walls that provide hunting perches and shelter. Look for them on sunny surfaces during warm days, as they're often seen basking on rocks, wooden structures, or plant stems.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter shelters under bark or in leaf litter. This is when you're most likely to spot them sunning themselves on warm surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with adults hunting actively during daylight hours. Mating displays and courtship behaviors are most commonly observed during warm summer days.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, but begin seeking winter shelter as temperatures drop. Egg sacs may be found tucked under bark or in protected crevices.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in silk-lined retreats under loose bark, in rock crevices, or within leaf litter. They remain dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Jumping spiders have better color vision than most mammals, including humans - they can see into the ultraviolet spectrum and use this super-vision to spot the UV-reflective silk draglines that other spiders leave behind as they move, essentially letting them 'see' the invisible highways their prey travels!
confusionNotes: Putnam's Jumping Spider is easily confused with other Phidippus jumping spiders, especially the more common Bold Jumping Spider. The key is looking at subtle differences in body proportions and markings rather than relying on size alone - when in doubt, note the habitat and take a photo to compare markings later.
contextualKnowledge: With only 11 recorded observations in New England, Putnam's Jumping Spider is either quite rare in our region or significantly under-reported. Many jumping spiders in the Phidippus genus look very similar, and positive identification often requires close examination or expert confirmation, so this species may be more common than records suggest.
compareHints: Putnam's Jumping Spider is part of a large genus of very similar-looking jumping spiders, making field identification challenging without close examination. Unlike the Bold Jumping Spider which has distinct white markings, or the Brilliant Jumping Spider with its metallic green chelicerae (mouthparts), Putnam's tends to have more subtle markings. The best approach is to photograph any Phidippus jumping spider you encounter, as distinguishing between species often requires comparing multiple characteristics that are difficult to assess in the field.
